title: Linearising graphs
examples: When should I use linearising graphs in my practical work?
How do I find the gradient from a curved graph?
What does it mean if my graph is not a straight line?

explain.say: Today we learn about linearising graphs in physics. Sometimes data does not make a straight line. We can change the graph to make it straight.

items: Changing graph to make it straight

explain.say: One common way is plotting the y value against the square of the x value. This is plotting y versus x squared. This transformation can reveal a simple relationship.
Another transformation involves using logarithms. You might plot the natural log of y against x. This is using the log scale effectively.
The gradient of a straight line has a specific meaning. It represents the rate of change between two variables. It tells you how much y changes for a unit change in x.

draw.text: Gradient = change in y / change in x

explain.say: For example, if we plot y versus x squared, the gradient found is related to the initial velocity. This helps us find a constant value easily.

items: y vs x² gradient relates to initial velocity

draw.text: Example: y vs x² gives velocity

faq.q: Why do I need to linearise a graph?
faq.a: You linearise a graph when the underlying physical relationship is simple. A straight line makes it easy to calculate constants from the gradient. You might also ask this as: How do I find a constant value from data? Or: Why can't I just use the curve?
asks: How do I find a constant value from data?
Why can't I just use the curve?

faq.q: What does the gradient actually represent?
faq.a: The gradient is the ratio of the change in the vertical axis to the change in the horizontal axis. It is the rate of change of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable. You might also ask this as: What is the slope of the line? Or: What does the gradient tell me?
asks: What is the slope of the line?
What does the gradient tell me?

faq.q: When should I plot y versus x squared?
faq.a: You should plot y versus x squared when the relationship is predicted to be proportional to the square of x. This is common in motion experiments involving distance and time squared. You might also ask this as: Is this always the right plot? Or: What if I use x squared?
asks: Is this always the right plot?
What if I use x squared?

faq.q: What if I use logarithms for linearising?
faq.a: Using logarithms helps linearise relationships that follow an exponential pattern. You are essentially transforming the curve into a straight line on a log-log plot. You might also ask this as: When is log useful? Or: How do I use logs in physics?
asks: How do I use logs in physics?

faq.q: Do I need to calculate the gradient by drawing a line?
faq.a: Ideally, you calculate the gradient using two points that are far apart on the straight line. Using the best-fit line or two distinct points is more accurate than estimating from the curve. You might also ask this as: What is the best way to find the gradient? Or: Can I use the ruler for the gradient?
asks: What is the best way to find the gradient?
Can I use the ruler for the gradient?

facts: The gradient is calculated as the change in the vertical axis divided by the change in the horizontal axis.
Linearising graphs transform non-linear data into a straight line for easier analysis.
Plotting y versus x squared is used when the relationship involves the square of x.
A straight line passing through the origin has a gradient equal to the ratio of the y value to the x value.

quiz.say: If a graph of pressure versus depth is curved, what transformation might linearise it?

options.show: Plotting the square root of pressure versus depth
options.say: Plotting the square root of pressure versus depth

options.show: Plotting the natural log of pressure against depth
options.say: Plotting the natural log of pressure against depth

quiz.why: This transformation is used because the physical law relating pressure and depth is exponential, making the log plot straight.

wrong.0: This changes the relationship incorrectly and does not match the expected physical law.
wrong.1: This keeps the data curved, which defeats the purpose of linearising the graph.
wrong.2: This is an arbitrary mathematical change and is not the standard transformation for this physical relationship.

quiz.say: A straight line plotted from a graph has a gradient of five. What does this mean?

options.show: The line passes through the point (1, 5).
options.say: The line passes through the point (1, 5).

options.show: For every one unit increase on the horizontal axis, the vertical axis increases
options.say: For every one unit increase on the horizontal axis, the vertical axis increases

options.show: The total change in y is five.
options.say: The total change in y is five.

quiz.why: The gradient is the ratio of the change in y to the change in x, so a gradient of five means y changes five times as much as x.

wrong.0: While it means the line is steep, this is a description, not the precise mathematical meaning of the gradient.
wrong.1: The gradient describes the slope everywhere, not just the point (1, 5).
wrong.3: The gradient is a ratio, not the total change, unless the change in x is exactly one unit.

quiz.say: To find the constant acceleration from a displacement-time graph, which plot should be linearised?

options.show: Plotting the square root of displacement versus time
options.say: Plotting the square root of displacement versus time

options.show: Plotting the gradient of the displacement-time graph
options.say: Plotting the gradient of the displacement-time graph

quiz.why: The relationship between displacement and time squared is linear when acceleration is constant, and the gradient gives twice the acceleration.

wrong.0: This plot is curved if the acceleration is constant, so it is not linear.
wrong.1: This transformation is not standard for determining constant acceleration from this type of data.
wrong.2: The gradient of the displacement-time graph is velocity, not the acceleration itself.
